claims.text: Chemical short-range order significantly suppresses lattice thermal conductivity in concentrated refractory high-entropy alloys relative to a random solid solution.
SRO enhances phonon scattering by increasing local chemical-potential fluctuations.
SRO produces static lattice distortions and local strain fields that scatter phonons.
Random concentrated alloys already have low lattice thermal conductivity because of mass variance and lattice distortion.
SRO creates periodic or semi-periodic chemical potentials that resonantly scatter phonons of particular wavelengths.
High-temperature homogenization followed by rapid quenching retains MoNbTaW in a random-solid-solution state.
An equilibrium SRO state in MoNbTaW can be defined at 800 K.
SRO is thermodynamically favorable in MoNbTaW over approximately 600–900 K.
The relevant SRO domains have negative Warren-Cowley ordering parameters and associated static atomic displacements.
The characteristic SRO-domain size is typically 1–2 nm.
Phonon scattering in the random alloy is dominated by mass variance and random strain fields.
SRO amplifies the severe-lattice-distortion effect by increasing local strain-field amplitudes beyond those of a random distribution.
SRO reduces both phonon group velocity and phonon mean free path.
The SRO sample will have lower lattice thermal conductivity than the RSS sample throughout 50–1000 K.
The SRO-induced suppression will be strongest at 300–600 K because phonon-phonon scattering is then less dominant than defect scattering.
Well-developed SRO will reduce lattice thermal conductivity by 10–20% relative to the RSS state.
The SRO sample will exhibit a flatter thermal-conductivity temperature dependence at intermediate temperatures.
The RSS state of a refractory high-entropy alloy typically has a thermal conductivity of 5–15 W/m·K.
If SRO evolves into phase-separated precipitates or long-range order, interface scattering becomes the dominant transport mechanism.
Near melting, anharmonic phonon-phonon scattering can mask the effect of SRO on lattice thermal conductivity.

contradictions.description: The proposed favorable annealing interval is 600–900 K, but the experiment anneals the SRO sample at 800°C (1073 K), outside that stated interval. This also conflicts with the repeatedly referenced 800 K equilibrium-SRO state.

The rule says that an increase in conductivity after annealing to dissolve SRO would falsify suppression. In fact, conductivity increasing when SRO is removed means the prior SRO state had lower conductivity, which supports the predicted suppression rather than falsifying it.
